meta.title: Launcher Trajectory Criticality Prediction using Recurrent Neural Networks
meta.authorsHtml: Arthur Péquin<sup>∗</sup>, Daniel Blanquez, Lionel Brayeur

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: The prediction of launcher trajectories is a central problem in aerospace engineering, as safety is at stake in the event of trajectory failure. The Autonomous Flight Safety System (AFSS), as an independent subsystem of launch vehicles, processes data from the onboard Global Positioning System (GPS) and the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensors to make flight termination decisions in the event of an errant vehicle. In an effort to improve on-flight mission control, this work reports on the integration of predictive machine learning (ML) models into the AFSS for the detection of launcher trajectory failures. Machine learning algorithms pertaining to the recurrent neural networks (RNNs) class are explored for their predictive capabilities in time-dependent problems. The models are trained and validated on data generated using a launcher flight simulator. All investigated models provide high global accuracies hence validating the approach. An inference time benchmark was performed on an embedded AMD Kria board to challenge the models in a practical environment for space mission control.

blocks.html: Predicting launcher trajectories with accuracy is key during launch operations to protect life and property. In an effort to improve reliability, the Autonomous Flight Safety System (AFSS) is capable of replacing human-in-the-loop systems or working in parallel with them [1]. The AFSS uses data from the onboard Global Positioning System (GPS) and the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) sensors to make flight termination decisions in the event of an errant vehicle [2]. The AFSS is configured prior to the mission in accordance with specific safety rules and contains algorithms that use tracking and attitude data from the launcher and mission diagnostics.

Launchers follow complex flight paths that are influenced by external factors such as environmental perturbations, aerodynamics and onboard control systems [3]. Small deviations at an early-stage of the flight can lead to critical situations that range from minor off-course deviations to trajectory and mission losses. It is therefore crucial to develop tools able to predict trajectory deviations and critical scenarios to allow early interventions or contingency plans during flights. Data-driven methods are foreseen to improve existing solutions in space applications [4, 5].

Machine learning algorithms [6], in particular recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have demonstrated prediction capabilities in time-series problems [7]. Recurrent neural networks are a class of neural networks specifically designed to handle sequential data. Conversely to standard artificial neural networks (ANNs), RNN architectures contain feedback loops that enable multiple input spots [8]. This feature enables the learning of temporal patterns within sequential data. In the context of launcher trajectory criticality prediction, RNNs are particularly suitable as the model can consider not only the current state of the launcher but also its past states to predict potential failure [9, 10].

The overarching goal of the present study is to develop a robust, interpretable, and efficient machine learning framework capable of predicting trajectory criticality. The project aims to leverage sequential models to capture temporal dependencies in launcher flight data and provide actionable predictions during different phases of the trajectory. The objective of the developed models is to determine whether a given trajectory will lead to a critical scenario within a forecast horizon. Here, “criticality” refers to whether a trajectory segment is likely to result in failure or deviation beyond acceptable safety bounds, e.g., entering a high-risk zone where a mission termination would endanger infrastructures or populations. The integration of predictive models into the AFSS is regarded as a long-term prospect and motivates this conceptual investigation.
The present work follows a structured workflow of a machine learning model development which contains several stages [6]: data generation, data processing, model development, training and validation.

The performance of any machine learning model heavily depends on the quality of its training data. As such, a launcher flight simulator was parametrised on physical measurements of a launch vehicle nominal trajectory to generate new trajectories with synthetic perturbations. Launcher trajectories are governed by deterministic physics such as Newtonian mechanics, aero-dynamical forces, and probabilistic perturbations, e.g., environmental variability [3]. Simulated trajectories differ from the nominal trajectory as a result of applied synthetic forces mimicking perturbations during flights. A perturbation model, inspired from a stochastic Dryden modelling approach for turbulence [11], has been developed and integrated in the simulator. A scaling factor, of values 1.0 to 500.0 in a distributed fashion, is applied on the synthetic perturbations to generate trajectories under perturbations of varying intensities. Although simplistic, this aimed at completing the trajectory database with synthetic yet physically representative samples for concept validation.

blocks.html: New perturbed simulations were generated with the simulator for a total trajectory time of 2000 s. Having a simulation timestep of 1 s, all trajectories therefore contain 2000 data points. Each trajectory point includes 16 features: spatial coordinates (x, y, z); attitude quaternion (qw, qx, qy, qz); velocities (vx, vy, vz); angular velocities (ωx, ωy, ωz); and angular accelerations (αx, αy, αz).

In the case of such a supervised-learning binary classification problem [12], trajectory data points must be labelled. A trajectory is considered critical when the launcher deviates from the nominal trajectory beyond acceptable safety bounds, potentially leading to mission failure, e.g., the launcher will enter high-risk and prohibited spatial regions. In the present study, the acceptable safety bounds are seen as a pre-defined collection of position coordinates around the nominal trajectory, shaped as a plume with three configurable parameters, e.g., the opening angles of cones at the beginning and end of the trajectory, and the trajectory time at which the cone stops expanding and starts shrinking.

Figure 1 presents several perturbed trajectories plotted on top of the nominal path and a plume-like confidence envelope of parameters 2°, 0.5° and 1500 s. This tolerance definition constraints the launcher to a more restricted area when approaching the final part of the trajectory, mimicking a scenario of more stringent regulations at mission-end, and serves as groundwork for more elaborated approaches. For the present study, a dataset is constructed consisting of 5 sets of 1000 simulated trajectories of 2000 timesteps each, i.e., 2.000.000 data points of 16 variables.

blocks.caption: Schematic representation of data sequencing with two parameters for sequence and forecast lengths, e.g., (5,1).
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The data points are then labelled by comparing their point-by-point distance with the corresponding xyzperturbed(t)∥at any time t, to the acceptance envelope radius r(t). Label at t is nominal (1) if d(t) ≤r(t) and critical (0) in case d(t) > r(t). In other words, a perturbed launcher is considered within the acceptance bounds at time t if it is located within a sphere of centre xyznominal(t) and of radius r(t). Statistics return that 83.9% of all labels are nominal, 16.1% are critical, with a trajectory failure rate, calculated as the ratio of trajectories ending with a critical label, of 67.2%. The trajectory data are then sequenced to provide suitable inputs and outputs to recurrent neural networks. Data also undergoes normalization, batching and dataset splitting steps, as generally done in machine learning datasets preparation [13].

Figure 2 presents the general idea behind the creation of sequential data where two parameters can be tuned, i.e., the sequence length which represents the number of timesteps of a trajectory contained within a time window sample; and the forecast length which is the number of timesteps separating the current, i.e., latest acquisition, time from the time of the state to predict. Changing the values of these parameters is an objective of the study to: i) reinforce the temporal awareness of the models by training on longer sequences; and ii) predict states longer in the future, i.e., earlier detections of failing trajectories. Several sequential datasets are created according to the coordinates (sequenceforecast) lengths. The features for the input dataset X are taken from t−sequence length+1 till time t whereas the labels y are taken at t+forecast length. All the 16 trajectory features are used as inputs. 80% of the X and y datasets are dedicated to training (Xtrain, ytrain) whereas 20% of the remaining data is used for testing/validation (Xtest, ytest). The percentage of critical labels in both datasets is preserved at 16.1% with a stratification method [13].

blocks.html: Recurrent neural networks are explored as their feedback loop principle is well suited for temporal sequences [8]. The model architectures consist in an input layer handling sequential data that will feed a recurrent layer. Besides vanilla RNNs, LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) and GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) models are also explored for the recurrent units [14]. The recurrent layer is connected to a fully connected dense layer before reaching the output layer. A ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) activation function [13] is used for the dense layer. A sigmoid activation function [13] is used on the output layer to convert inputs into values between 0 and 1, which is suitable for binary classification problems [12]. The final output of the model, i.e., a float between 0 and 1, is turned into a binary by applying a 0.5 threshold on the output value. A value below or equal to the threshold is turned into a false boolean, i.e., 0 (critical status). All values strictly above the threshold are returned as positive booleans, i.e., 1 (nominal status).

Table 1 presents the ML model parameters for their implementation in PyTorch [15]. Training is performed using NVIDIA GPU resources and a binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss function is used in the context of binary classification problems:

The choice of machine learning models appertaining to the RNN class is further motivated by the resources constraints of spatial on-board equipment. Lightweight solutions are prioritised and heavier alternatives, such as transformers or deep neural networks (DNN) [16], would hardly meet these real-time calculations requirements.

blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: This section presents the performance evaluation of the RNN, LSTM, and GRU models trained and tested on the different sequential datasets of the sequence-forecast lengths map, and aims at validating the conceptual use of machine learning algorithms for generic failure detections in launcher trajectories.

Figure 3 presents the training and testing learning curves, i.e., losses, for an example of RNN model. This model learns how to predict the status of the launcher trajectory 1 s ahead of time with around 99% global accuracy on the training and testing datasets. The model predictions are turned from probabilities into binaries by applying the 0.5 threshold and then compared to the true labels. The global accuracy is defined as the fraction of correct predictions over 50000 test samples.

Figure 4 reports the global accuracies of the investigated RNN, LSTM and GRU models at several entries of the sequence length – forecast length map. For short sequences, i.e., a sequence length of 5, and short forecast lengths, i.e., 1 s and 5 s, all models return an accuracy above 99.5%, with the best results obtained using a simple RNN approach. While increasing the sequence length, more data are fed to the network and LSTMs show better prediction capabilities. The reinforced ability to learn patterns from time series is demonstrated in the results of the LSTM models by increasing the forecast length from a couple of seconds up to 10 minutes, i.e., 600 seconds. It is clear that it becomes more and more difficult to predict the future status of the launcher given information at current time. The accuracies decrease from above 99.5% to 93.2% for the RNN and the GRU models, and 94.1% for an LSTM model.

The comparison of multiple sequence lengths and forecast horizons was conducted solely as part of a prospective model selection study aimed at identifying the most suitable architecture and temporal configuration. In an operational setting, only the best-performing model would be deployed, and therefore a single window size and forecast horizon would be used.

blocks.title: On the on-board validity of the approach

blocks.html: Beyond accuracy, the developed models must deliver reasonable computational times in order to be deployed. The mean inference time, i.e., the average time needed for a model to produce one prediction, is estimated on the CPU resources of an AMD Kria board resembling an on-board configuration.

blocks.html: Focusing on the most performing models, Table 2 presents the mean inference times over 50000 samples of RNN and LSTM models obtained on the CPU resources of the Kria board. With scarce resources, inference times are LSTM models benefit from highly optimized kernels in reduced environments. LSTMs are the best modelling options as they combine the highest global accuracies with the shortest inference times. On average, it can be concluded that all the models are able to infer a prediction within about 10 ms on a computational set-up resembling an on-board configuration, which is lower than an estimate of a limiting value of 15 ms for embedded hardware to ensure real-time execution. The highest inference times for each model are approximately 2.89 times the mean values. Only LSTM models meet the hardware requirements for all samples. Optimization strategies, e.g., sequence truncation, or feature pruning through feature importance methods [17] are recommended for on-board development to further reduce the computational needs of the machine learning models.

The present study investigated the use of recurrent neural networks to predict the criticality of launcher trajectories. The overarching goal of the project was to determine with accuracy whether a launcher, at any point on its trajectory, is likely to maintain a nominal pathway or enter a critical state that would trigger response procedures. A complete framework has been designed for the implementation, training and evaluation of predictive machine learning algorithms. Trajectories were simulated to enrich the datasets used to train and test the models. A stochastic synthetic force was applied during flights to reproduce the natural variability of ascent launcher dynamics. Trajectories beyond predefined safety radii were labelled as critical. Data was processed, sequenced and split to provide useful information for the learning task of temporal patterns. Three classes of recurrent neural networks have been investigated with configurable hidden sizes, dropout layers, and fully connected output heads. Experiments were carried out across multiple sequence lengths and forecast horizons to assess how temporal context influences models’ predictive capabilities.

All presented models provide high global accuracies. An inference time benchmark was performed on the CPUs of an embedded AMD Kria board. Contrary to expectations, some hardware configurations showed LSTM models outperforming simpler RNNs. This suggested that optimized kernel implementations and memory access patterns deeply influence embedded systems’ inference speed. This workflow was designed to tackle the practical challenges of developing deployable predictive models for space mission control. The present study can be summarized in the following points:

• model architecture selection plays a crucial role in the prediction and computational performances. RNNs are computationally lighter whereas LSTMs demonstrate higher predictive capabilities when fed with more input data. All architectures ensure at least 93% accuracy regardless of the forecast length considered.
This accuracy goes up to 99.2% for predictions within the next 3 minutes;
• algorithms demonstrated low-latency performance, i.e., less than 10ms, when benchmarked on embedded systems like an AMD Kria board. This suggests a strong potential for on-board deployment;
• the selection of input features can be tailored after a prospective study. Feature importance methods can be used to discard unnecessary variables and alleviate the architectures complexities;

• the framework developed in the present study is highly adjustable, allowing the rapid incorporation of improved trajectory simulations, and the training of updated models to further improve the predictive performance in realistic conditions. The validation of the models on synthetically noisy or real flight data is seen as a valuable prospect to assess the models’ sensitivity.

Finally, deployment with ONNX and ONNX Run-time [18] presents a promising path toward integration with real-world embedded avionics systems where inference efficiency and certification requirements are stringent.
